transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. I'm Dr. [name]. To start, can you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Well… mostly I’m here because I just can’t seem to keep my mind on one thing anymore. It’s gotten to where I’ll be trying to do something, even something I know how to do—I've been a carpenter a long time—and the littlest thing pulls me off. Like if one saw starts up nearby, or somebody walks past the office, or I suddenly think, “Oh, I’ve got to check on that other job,” then I’m gone. My attention just snaps away.

And then I’ll realize later that I never got back to what I was supposed to be doing, or the whole day has kind of slipped out from under me. It’s frustrating because it’s not that I don’t care or don’t know what needs doing. I do. I just… I can’t seem to stay with it. One interruption, even just a thought in my own head, and I’m off track.
Did you notice this kind of trouble staying focused back when you were a kid or teenager, or is this something that's really only started recently?

No, it definitely goes way back. I mean, it’s worse now, or maybe it matters more now because there’s more responsibility, but I can remember it even in grade school—before I was 12, for sure.

My teachers used to tell my mother the same thing over and over, that I was bright, but careless. That was the word they used a lot. I’d lose homework or leave it half-done, or I’d forget what the instructions were right after they gave them. And I wasn’t trying to be difficult. I’d be sitting there at my desk, supposed to be finishing something, and I’d just be staring out the window or watching something else in the room, and then everyone else would be done and I’d barely have started.

My mother would get these comments like, “She’s smart, she just needs to apply herself,” and I remember feeling embarrassed because I didn’t know how to explain that I meant to do it. I really did. I just… didn’t stay with it. So no, it’s not brand new. It’s been there since I was little.
Growing up and even now, do you notice yourself feeling restless, fidgety, or having trouble sitting still, or acting impulsively without thinking things through?

Yeah, I do get that, especially the restless part. I wouldn’t say I’m bouncing off the walls or anything, but if I have to sit still for too long, it’s like I get wound up inside.

The desk work is the worst for that—doing estimates, paperwork, sitting there trying to go line by line. I know I need to just stay in the chair and finish it, and it’s not like I physically can’t. My wrist is healed now, so there isn’t really an excuse like before. But I’ll be sitting there and my whole body feels like it wants to get up and move around. Same thing in long meetings. I’ll tell myself, “Just sit here, listen, get through it,” but inside I feel kind of trapped, like I need to stand up or walk somewhere or do something with my hands.

It’s been that way for a long time, I think. I can make myself stay put when I have to, but it takes a lot out of me, and I’m fighting that urge the whole time.
Do you often find yourself interrupting others in conversation, blurting out answers before someone finishes a question, or having trouble waiting your turn in situations like lines or traffic?

I’m not really sure on that one. I mean, I don’t think of myself as someone who’s always cutting people off or blurting things out. Maybe I have here and there—everybody probably does sometimes—but it’s not the thing people complain about with me, if that makes sense.

Waiting in lines or traffic… I don’t love it, but I can wait. I might get irritated like anyone else, especially if I’m already running behind, but I don’t usually do something rash or push ahead or anything like that. In conversations, I try to let people finish. Sometimes I might lose the thread of what I was going to say if I wait too long, so I may jump in a little sooner than I should, but I wouldn’t say it’s a big pattern that I’ve noticed.

So… I guess my answer is, not especially. Not compared to the other stuff.
Can you tell me about how these attention and restlessness issues have affected other areas of your life outside of work—like at home, in relationships, or with other responsibilities?

Yeah… it’s definitely not just work, though work is where it shows up the most clearly because there are consequences right away. Like if I mess up an estimate, or I forget to order something, or I put off calling someone back because I keep thinking I’ll do it in a minute and then the whole day is gone—that can cost me. I’ve lost commissions that way, and I’ve had jobs where we had to redo things because I missed a detail or didn’t follow through on some part of the scheduling.

And the crew notices. They’re not cruel about it, but I can tell they don’t want to depend on me for certain things now. If it’s ordering materials or keeping the schedule straight, people kind of double-check me or just go around me, and honestly I don’t blame them, but it feels awful. I’ve been doing this work a long time, so it’s embarrassing to feel like the unreliable one.

At home, my husband has picked up a lot of the slack. Bills, reminders, paperwork—he handles more of that now because if it’s on me, papers get misplaced, or I miss the thing that needed to be done, or I set something down “just for now” and then it disappears. He’ll ask me if I took care of something, and I’ll have this horrible sinking feeling because I meant to, but I either forgot or I can’t find the letter or the notice or whatever it was.

It causes tension, not always big blowups, but that steady frustration. I feel like I’m making other people carry the boring but important stuff because I can’t keep it together consistently. And I hate that, because I’m not trying to be careless. It just keeps happening.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient reports longstanding, childhood-onset (pre-age 12) difficulties with sustained attention (easily distracted, careless errors, forgetfulness, difficulty completing tasks) alongside hyperactive-restless symptoms (internal restlessness, difficulty remaining seated, need to move) that have persisted into adulthood. These symptoms cause clear functional impairment across multiple domains (occupational performance, marital/home responsibilities). Impulsivity symptoms (interrupting, blurting, poor turn-taking) are minimal/subthreshold, but the combination of significant inattentive and hyperactive symptoms with childhood onset and cross-situational impairment supports a diagnosis of ADHD, combined presentation (ICD-10 F90.0 - Disturbance of activity and attention).
